correctness.rationale: PASS: For arbitrary a.s. finite threshold law, stop at first boundary contact in the open state. The strong Markov property factors the no-reset Laplace transforms as h_j=c_j Φ with identical Φ>0. Solving the two-state backward ODE gives c_0,c_1 explicitly. The surviving gate-state kernel R=(I-he_1^T)(rI-Q)^(-1) is derived by decomposing at absorption, and 2x2 inversion gives a delay ratio independent of Φ, strictly positive. The Robin specialization matches an independent coupled finite-difference generator solve at five parameter points; symbolic identities and ten further arbitrary-threshold matrix checks pass. The finite tests supplement, not replace, proof.

originality.rationale: PASS (qualified): The instantaneous-absorption formula is explicitly published by Mercado-Vásquez & Boyer (2021, Appendix B Eq.49), so that numerical equality is not claimed original. Bressloff (2022) permits general contact-threshold distributions under complete refresh, but does not compare retaining versus resampling gate state at such thresholds. The added assertion is a nontrivial law-universality across all finite threshold distributions, established by a common hitting-transform factor and a separate gate-state renewal kernel. Close and broad possible implicit coverage is disclosed.
residual_risks: The perfect-absorber formula is already published verbatim in 2021; only the arbitrary threshold-law invariance is assessed as additional.
An abstract Markov-renewal theorem or inverse-local-time result could implicitly subsume the extension even if the searched papers do not state it.
Nonexponential reaction laws require resetting threshold/contact progress on both protocols; retaining the threshold changes the model and may break the identity.
Independent publication-priority and proof audits remain necessary.

value.rationale: PASS: A physically motivated mechanistic distinction between conformational memory and chemical contact progress yields a sharp, positive reset penalty that is invariant under the entire (including non-Markovian) surface reaction threshold law. This shows that altering surface chemistry changes each first-passage mean but not their difference. It generalizes a known perfectly reactive observation into a structural independence principle and identifies precisely which reset protocol features can affect it.
